data.text: Description of Zygosaccharomyces progenitor A Pontes, MR Silva, D Rutkowski, C Carvalho, RL Vannette, JP Sampaio sp. nov.

Etymology: pro.geni.tor. L. masc. n. progenitor, meaning ancestor or parent, and referring to the role of this species as a parental contributor in the origin of multiple interspecies hybrids within the genus Zygosaccharomyces.

After 7days of growth on YM agar at 25C, the streak culture is cream-coloured, and colonies have entire margins, convex elevation and are wrinkled with a cerebriform, dull surface. After 3days of growth in YM broth at 25C, the cells are globose to sub-globose (3459 m) and occur singly or in pairs (Fig. 2a). Reproduction is by multilateral budding. On Dalmau plates incubated at 25C, pseudohyphae or true hyphae were not observed after 2weeks. Sporulation was observed on acetate agar after 48weeks of incubation at 20C. Asci are persistent and normally formed after conjugation of two separate cells or after conjugation of a cell and its bud (Fig. 2bg). Ascospores are spherical, with one to four formed per ascus.

The physiological characterization was based on strains PYCC 7198T, PYCC 9375, PYCC 10391, PYCC 10392, PYCC 10393 and PYCC 10394. d-glucose and maltose were fermented. Sucrose, --trehalose, melibiose, lactose, cellobiose, melezitose and raffinose were not fermented. Assimilation of carbon compounds: d-glucose, d-galactose (positive or weak), maltose (positive or delayed), glycerol (positive or weak), xylitol (delayed or negative), d-glucitol (positive or delayed), d-mannitol, galactitol (variable) and d-glucono-1,5-lactone (variable). Carbon compounds not assimilated: l-sorbose, N-acetyl-d-glucosamine, d-ribose, d-xylose, d-arabinose, l-arabinose, l-rhamnose, sucrose, --trehalose, -methyl-d-glucoside, cellobiose, salicin, melibiose, lactose, raffinose, melezitose, inulin, starch, erythritol, ribitol, d-glucitol, myo-inositol, d-gluconate, d-glucuronate, dl-lactate, succinate, citrate, methanol, ethanol, l-malic acid and l-tartaric acid. Nitrogen compounds assimilated: ethylamine, l-lysine and cadaverine. Nitrogen compounds not assimilated: nitrate, nitrite, creatine and creatinine. Variable ability to grow in the presence of 10% (sodium chloride) NaCl. Unable to grow in the presence of 0.01% and 0.1% cycloheximide and without vitamins. Starch-like compounds were not produced. Hydrolysis of urea and the diazonium blue B reaction were negative. Growth was positive at 37C and negative at 40C.

The holotype (PYCC 7198h) is permanently maintained in a metabolically inactive state in the Portuguese Yeast Culture Collection, Caparica, Portugal, and ex-holotype cultures were deposited in the same collection (PYCC 7198) and in the Yeast Collection of the Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute, Utrecht, the Netherlands (CBS 19066). The MycoBank accession number is 859833. PYCC 7198 was isolated from a soil sample collected underneath an olive tree (Olea europaea) in Mao, Santarm, Portugal, in November 2016. The whole-genome data were deposited at DDBJ/ENA/GenBank under the following identifiers: Bioproject ID PRJEB92122 and BioSample IDs SAMEA118697206SAMEA118697217. The ITS sequences extracted from the whole-genome data are available on Figshare (DOI: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.29636912.v1).

Salient physiological differences between the novel species and its closest relatives are few. Typically, Zygosaccharomyces species assimilate a limited number of carbon and nitrogen compounds, which complicates the detection of physiological differences between species. We compared the physiological profile of Z. progenitor sp. nov. with those of its closest relatives, Z. mellis, Z. osmophilus, Z. rouxii and Z. siamensis. Z. osmophilus is the most osmophilic species in this group. Its preference for elevated sugar concentrations results in poor growth in a glucose medium with the standard 0.5% sugar concentration (Table 2). For the remaining species, the ability to grow on erythritol distinguishes Z. siamensis from Z. progenitor, and Z. mellis is unable to grow at 37C, contrary to Z. progenitor (Table 2). Distinguishing Z. rouxii from Z. progenitor based on physiological characteristics appears not possible, as the two species have identical physiological profiles except for a few variable tests of Z. rouxii.

To investigate if additional evidence for the detection of Z. progenitor is available, we used D1/D2 and ITS sequences of Z. progenitor as queries for searches in the GenBank database. The top 100 sequences from each blastN search were retrieved and analysed in detail. Our results are shown in Table S2. After discarding duplicates, possible hybrids and sequences that matched those of Z. progenitor less confidently (labelled in Table S2 as Zygosaccharomyces cf. progenitor), we identified 32 possible additional representatives, either cultures or sequences based on environmental DNA. Among these sequences that we confidently assigned to Z. progenitor, approximately one-third (ten) corresponded to cultures obtained from honey of A. mellifera or from Bombus; another third (nine) corresponded to direct detection without culturing in a single industrial substrate (probiotic production reactor for use in shrimp farming); and the final third had unknown sources (four) or originated from plants or soil (three) and soy sauce (four).

Contrary to Z. rouxii, which is mostly found in anthropic environments such as grape must, fruit syrups and jams, or soy sauce, Z. progenitor sp. nov. is mostly found in natural substrates. Although the number of isolates of Z. progenitor sp. nov. is limited, an association with social bees of the genera Apis (which includes the common honeybees) and Bombus (the bumblebees) might be hypothesized, and future studies should aim to test this possibility. As both bees and bumblebees produce honey, and several cultures of the new species were isolated directly from honey, the hypothesis that Z. progenitor is ecologically associated with honey should also be tested. It is also relevant to notice that some isolates were found in distinct environments such as soil and flowers, suggesting some degree of ubiquity or a more generalist ecology. It would be interesting to compare the degree of ecological specialization within Zygosaccharomyces, testing, at one extreme, the apparent generalist strategy of Z. rouxii and, at the other, the specialist ecologies of Z. favi and Z. siamensis, which are found only in honey [3, 6]. Such inquiries would be important to shed light on the natural ecology of Zygosaccharomyces, a mostly unknown subject. Judging from the limited number of confirmed isolates of this novel species available at present, Z. progenitor sp. nov. appears to occur in temperate regions, in Europe (Portugal), Asia (Japan) and North America (USA).

Vanderwaltozyma osmotolerans (os.mo.to'le.rans. Gr. masc. n. osmos, a pushing; L. pres. part. tolerans, tolerating; N.L. part. adj. osmotolerans, osmotolerant).

After 3days at 25C on the YM agar, cells are elliptical (1335m) and occur singly or in pairs (Fig. 2a). The colonies are white to cream-coloured, buttery, raised and smooth, with entire margins. The organism does not form hyphae or pseudohyphae under any tested conditions, including on CMA medium. In YPD liquid medium, sediment forms after 1month, but no pellicle is observed. On acetate agar and V8A (1:1) at 25C for 2weeks, unconjugated asci containing typically four globose to short-ellipsoidal ascospores (1223m) are produced (Fig. 2b, c). d-Glucose and d-fructose are fermented, whereas d-galactose, sucrose, maltose, lactose, raffinose, trehalose and d-xylose are not fermented (Table 3). The carbon compounds assimilated are d-glucose, d-mannose, inulin, sucrose, d-galactose, trehalose (weak and slow) and d-fructose. The organism does not assimilate the following compounds: l-sorbose, d-xylose, l-arabinose, d-arabinose, d-ribose, cellobiose, salicin, lactose, maltose, raffinose, starch, glycerol, erythritol, ribitol, galactitol, d-mannitol, d-glucitol, xylitol, l-arabitol, d-arabitol, methanol, ethanol, dl-lactate, succinate, citrate, d-glucosamine, N-acetyl-d-glucosamine and gluconate. The only nitrogen compound assimilated is ammonium sulphate. However, nitrate, nitrite, l-lysine, d-glucosamine, N-acetyl-d-glucosamine and imidazole are not assimilated. Growth occurs at 1530 Cand is absent at 35C. Growth is observed in a broth containing 10% sodium chloride and 5% glucose, and in a broth containing 50% (w/v) glucose and 0.5% yeast extract. Growth is also observed on amino acid-free medium. No growth is observed in broths containing 0.01% or 0.1% cycloheximide, 15% sodium chloride and 5% glucose, 60% (w/v) glucose and 0.5% yeast extract or 1% acetic acid. Starch-like compounds are not produced. All three yeast strains tested in this study exhibited similar physiological characteristics, although slight differences in growth rates were noted among the strains.

Cells are Gram-staining-negative rods. Oxidase and catalase are positive. The predominant quinone is ubiquinone Q-8. Major cellular fatty acids (>10%) are summed feature 3 (C16:17c/6c), summed feature 8 (C18:17c/6c) and C16:0. The DNA G+C content of the type strain of the type species is 48.2 mol%. Puribacter membranae (mem.branae. L. gen. n. membranae, of a membrane, referring to the isolation source of the type strain from a membrane biofilm of a sewage treatment bioreactor).

Cells are Gram-stain-negative, non-spore-forming, non-motile rods, ~0.60.8m wide and 1.02.0m long. Colonies on LB agar are circular, convex (lens-shaped), smooth, cream-coloured and ~12mm in diameter after 48h of incubation at 30C. Growth occurs at 2837Cand pH 7.09.0. Growth is observed under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions. Catalase and oxidase reactions are positive. Acid or gas production from glucose fermentation is observed, and oxidation-fermentation tests of glucose are both positive. In API 20 NE, API 20 E and API 50CH tests, assimilation of glucose, maltose, galactose, fructose, sucrose, trehalose, d-turanose, gluconate, dl-malic acid, glycerol and ribose is observed. In the API 20 NE, API 20E, and API ZYM tests, positive enzymatic reactions were observed for nitrate reduction, -galactosidase, cytochrome oxidase, oxidase, nitrite production, alkaline phosphatase, C4 esterase, leucine arylamidase, acid phosphatase, and -glucosidase, with weakly positive reactions for C8 esterase lipase and naphthol-AS-BI-phosphohydrolase. Major cellular fatty acids (>10%) are summed feature 3 (C16:17c/6c), summed feature 8 (C18:17c/6c) and C16:0. The quinone system is ubiquinone Q-8. The DNA G+C content of the type strain is 48.2mol%. The type strain HTMS3T (NBRC 117344T=LMG 34133T) was isolated from a sewage treatment MBR at the Nagaoka Central Sewage Treatment Center, Nagaoka City, Niigata Prefecture, Japan (37 28 55 N 138 51 16 E). The GenBank/EMBL/DDBJ accession numbers for the 16S rRNA gene sequence and the nearly complete genome sequence of strain HTMS3T are LC877500 and AP040167.

Colony diameter and culture characteristics (14 days, 25C in the dark, in mm): Colonies on PDA attaining 13mm diameter, slightly radial, raised with crateriform centre, velvety, olive-grey (107), undulate white and entire margins; reverse olive-yellow (89). On OA attaining 20mm diameter, flat and slightly crateriform, velvety, olive-grey (107), white and entire margins; reverse olive-yellow (89). On PCA attaining 21mm diameter, slightly crateriform, olive-grey (107), slightly undulate white and entire margins; reverse olive-yellow (89). On DG 18, attaining 13mm diameter, slightly radial and crateriform, salmon coloration (41), entire margins; reverse ochreous (44).

Micromorphological characteristics (14days, on PDA, 25C in the dark): The superficial mycelium consists of hyaline, septate, branched hyphae with smooth walls, rarely presenting conidiophores in the hyphal coil. Conidiophores are hyaline, slightly dilated, subcylindrical, septate, smooth, (2.4)4.17(9.7)  (2.0)2.43.6(4) m wide (n=30). Conidiogenous cells annellide-like arising directly from the hyphae, hyaline to light brown, cylindrical, pear-shaped, with narrow apices, solitary or terminal, with a truncated base, hyaline to darker brown (when older), smooth, branched (25) or not. Conidia are globose to subglobose, (3.0)4.04.5(5.4) m (n=30), smooth and hyaline to subhyaline and can be isolated or in chains of up to 11 conidia. Sexual morphs not observed.
GenBank numbers: URM 9060T and URM 9061, PV477290, PV477291 (ITS), PV477288, PV477289 (LSU), PV477855, PV477856 (tef1), and PV477853 and PV477854 (tub2).

Notes: M. luziarum is phylogenetically closely related to M. micronesiensis (Woudenberg et al. 2016), M. brunneosporus (Sandoval-Denis et al. 2016) and M. chinensis (Jagielski et al. 2016). Morphologically, M. luziarum can be distinguished from closely related species by its slow growth on OA at 25C after 14 days (20mm M. luziarum, 1517mm for M. micronesiensis, 2125 for M. brunneosporus and 2528mm for M. chinensis). The new species differs in the size of conidiophores: M. luziarum [(2.4)4.17(9.7)  (2.0)2.43.6(4) m], M. brunneosporus (5151.52.5m) and M. micronesiensis [(6)711(14) m22.5(3) m]. Additionally, it presents differences in the shape and size of conidia among M. luziarum (globose or subglobose, (3.0)4.04.5(5.4) m), M. brunneosporus (subglobose or ellipsoidal, 452.55m), M. chinensis (ellipsoidal, 2423.5m) and M. micronesiensis (obovoid, 34(4.5)  (2) 2.53(3.5) m).

Microbaculum mangrovi (man.grovi. L. gen. n. mangrovi, of a mangrove, where the type strain was isolated). Cells are strictly aerobic, Gram-stain-negative, motile and ovoid- to rod-shaped, ~0.30.7 m in width and 0.93.2 m in length. Bacterial flagella are observed. Growth occurs at temperatures between 20 and 40 C (optimum 35 C) at pH 5.59.0 (optimum pH 6.07.0) with 09% (w/v) NaCl (optimum 12%). Starch and casein are not hydrolysed. In the API 20NE test, nitrate can be reduced to nitrite. The hydrolyzation of gelatin and aesculin was observed. In the Biolog GEN III MicroPlate test, d-fructose-6-PO4, glucuronamide, -hydroxy-d,l-butyric acid and acetoacetic acid are utilized as the sole carbon source. The utilization of d-turanose, d-salicin, d-fucose, l-fucose, d-galacturonic acid, l-galactonic acid lactone, d-glucuronic acid, -ketoglutaric acid, l-malic acid and acetic acid was observed. Sensitivity to minocycline, vancomycin, nalidixic acid, aztreonam and sodium butyrate. In the API ZYM test, the following enzyme activities are detected, including alkaline phosphatase, esterase (C4), esterase lipase (C8), lipase (C14), leucine arylamidase, valine arylamidase, cystine arylamidase, trypsin, -chymotrypsin, acid phosphatase and naphthol-AS-BI-phosphohydrolase. Q-10 was the respiratory quinone. C19:0 cyclo 8c and summed feature 8 (C18:1 7c and/or C18:1 6c) are the main fatty acids (>10%). The polar lipid profile contains DPG, PG, PE, PC, AL, PL1-5 and GL1-2. The DNA G+C content is 65.90mol%. The type strain is FT89T (=MCCC 1K08485T=KCTC 8079T), isolated from mangrove sediment in Shenzhen, China.

The GenBank/EMBL/DDBJ accession numbers for the 16S rRNA gene sequence and the draft genome sequence of strain FT89T are PV873149 and JBPODT000000000, respectively. The genomes from the current study have been deposited in eLMSG (an eLibrary of Microbial Systematics and Genomics, https://www.biosino.org/elmsg/index) under accession number LMSG_G000055147.1.

Bradyrhizobium monzae (monzae. N.L. gen. n. monzae, of Monza, named in honour of the Uruguayan Dr. Jorge Monza for his valuable contributions to the development of rhizobiology).

Cells are Gram-stain-negative, aerobic and non-spore-forming rods. Colonies on YMA at pH 7.0 are circular and beige, with 1mm in diameter. The strain Oc8T grows between 15 and 37C, with optimal growth at 28C. The pH range for growth is 5 to 8, with optimal growth at pH 7.0 and growth was observed up to 0.1% NaCl. Utilization as carbon sources of glycerol, d-xylose, d-galactose, d-glucose, d-fructose, d-mannose, d-mannitol, cellobiose, maltose, citrate, asparagine and glutamate was positive. Assimilation of d-inositol, d-sorbitol, raffinose and carboxymethylcellulose was negative. Assimilation of fucose was weakly positive. The strain is resistant to ampicillin and sensitive to chloramphenicol, neomycin, streptomycin, spectinomycin, kanamycin, vancomycin, erythromycin and tetracycline. The major cellular fatty acids are those from summed feature 8 (C18:16c/C18:17c) and C16:0. The new species can be differentiated from its closest related species of Bradyrhizobium based on ANI and dDDH analyses. The DNA G+C content of the strain is 63.27mol%. The GenBank accession numbers for the 16S rRNA gene sequence and the genome assembly are PP716865 and GCA_021458635, respectively.
The type strain Oc8T (=LMG 33261T=CECT 30885T) was isolated from a nodule of Crotalaria ochroleuca grown in Uruguay, and it belongs to the symbiovar cyanophyllae.

Amycolatopsis rhizosphaerihabitans (rhi.zo.sphae.ri.habi.tans. N.L. fem. n. rhizosphaera, the rhizosphere; L. pres. part. habitans, inhabiting; N.L. fem. part. adj. rhizosphaerihabitans, inhabiting the rhizosphere).

Aerobic, Gram-stain-positive actinobacterium that forms white aerial mycelia and cream colour substrate hyphae on Reasoners 2A medium, differentiating into a branched spore chain consisting of long or short stem spores with smooth surfaces. Well-developed substrate mycelium and white aerial mycelium are formed on all tested media. No diffusible pigment is produced on all tested media. Positive for HS production, gelatin liquefaction, aesculin hydrolysis, catalase production and Tween 20/40/60 degradation, but negative for milk solidification, nitrate reduction, Tween 80 degradation and starch hydrolysis. Growth occurred at 1247C (optimal at 30C), pH 5.010.0 (optimal at pH 7.0) and 06%NaCl (optimal at 01%). Cellobiose, d-trehalose, d-galactose, lactose, d-fructose, d-glucose, mannitol, inositol, ribose, d-raffinose, arabinose and l-xylose can be utilized as a sole carbon source, but not for d-sorbitol, l-rhamnose and sucrose. The following substances such as hydroxyproline, phenylalanine, l-threonine, l-tyrosine, valine, isoleucine, l-serine, lysine, l-histidine, asparagine and creatine can act as a sole nitrogen source, but not for l-aspartic acid, glutamic acid, l-arginine and methionine. The cell-wall diamino acid contains meso-DAP, and the whole-cell sugars contain galactose and mannose. The polar lipids consisted of DPG, PE, PI and PIM (Fig. S1). The dominant menaquinones were MK-9 (H4), MK-9 (H2) and MK-9 (H6). The major fatty acids (>10%) were C17:16c, summed feature 3 (C16:16c and/or C16:17c), iso-C16:0, iso-C15:0 and iso-C14:0.

The type strain, cg13T (=KCTC 59393T=MCCC 1K09229T), isolated from the rhizosphere soil of C. parasiticus collected in Xiangtan city, China. The DNA G+C content of the type strain genome is 69.1%. The GenBank accession numbers for the 16S rRNA gene and genome sequences of strain cg13T were PV635606 and CP166848, respectively.

Ferrigenium straubiae (straubi.ae. N.L. gen. n. straubiae, named after Kristina Straub in honour of her original isolation of the enrichment culture KS). The cells are slightly curved rods (0.72m) and are Gram-negative. This mesophilic, neutrophilic, non-halophilic organism grows autotrophically under microoxic conditions, using Fe(II) from FeS as the electron donor and O as the electron acceptor in agarose-stabilized medium. Cultured under this condition, the bacterium was non-stalk-forming, and a flagellum could not be observed using SEM. Growth occurs at 2030C (optimum 25C) and pH 6.07.5 (optimum 6.57.0). It does not utilize hydrogen, thiosulphate, sulphide, nitrite, nitrate, Mn+, glucose, acetate, pyruvate or citrate as an energy source. This bacterium belongs to the Gallionellaceae family, and the type strain is KS (DSM 118991, KCTC 25982). Strain KS was isolated from the 26-year-old laboratory-maintained enrichment culture KS, which was originally collected from freshwater sediment in Bremen, Germany (53.10971N 8.84510 E).

The bacterium has two distinct copies of the 16S rRNA gene, the full-length sequences gained from Illumina sequencing are deposited at GenBank under the accession numbers PV740118 and PV740119 and the partial sequences gained from Sanger sequencing are under the accession numbers PV739805, PV739806, PV739807 and PV739808. Additionally, the full-length 16S rRNA genes were annotated in the IMG database and can be accessed using the following gene IDs: 8132340740 and 8132340651 [48, 49].

Huang et al. [6] initially proposed the new taxon as Candidatus Ferrigenium straubiae based on a phylogenetic analysis that differentiated closely related taxa. Table 2 lists phenotypic and genotypic comparisons to closely related strains.

Apilactobacillus intestinapis (in.tes.tin.apis. L. neut. adj. intestinum, gut; L. fem. n. apis, a bee; N.L. gen. n. intestinapis, of the intestine of a bee).

Cells are Gram-stain-positive, catalase-negative, facultatively anaerobic, occurring as single, non-motile rods, 0.30.51.62.0 m in size. Growth was possible at 2537C, only weakly at 45C, and not at 10C. The strain grows in 15% NaCl and within a pH range of 4.010.0. Acid is produced from d-glucose, d-fructose, mannitol, sucrose, d-raffinose and gluconate, and weakly from 5-keto-gluconate. Acid is not produced from galactose, d-mannose, N-acetylglucosamine, amygdalin, arbutin, salicin, cellobiose, maltose, lactose, melibiose, trehalose, -gentiobiose, glycerol, ribose, sorbitol, erythritol, l-arabinose, d-arabinose, d-xylose, l-xylose, adonitol, -methyl-xyloside, l-sorbose, rhamnose, dulcitol, inositol, -methyl-d-mannoside, -methyl-d-glucoside, inulin, melezitose, starch, glycogen, xylitol, d-turanose, d-lyxose, d-fucose, l-fucose, d-arabitol, l-arabitol, d-tagatose or 2-keto-gluconate. Aesculin is not hydrolysed. Alkaline phosphatase, leucine arylamidase, valine arylamidase, cystine arylamidase, -chymotrypsin and acid phosphatase activities are detected, but no activities for esterase (C4), esterase lipase (C8), lipase (C14), trypsin, -galactosidase, -galactosidase, -glucuronidase, -glucosidase, naphthol-AS-BI-phosphohydrolase, -glucosidase, N-acetyl--glucosaminidase, -mannosidase or -fucosidase are detected. Strain 1-1-2T (=BCRC 81468T=NBRC 117233T) was designated as the type strain, isolated from the gut of a honeybee (A. mellifera). The GenBank/EMBL/DDBJ accession numbers for the 16S rRNA and genome sequence of strain 1-1-2T (=BCRC 81468T=NBRC 117233T) are LC856627 and JBMHFD000000000, respectively.

Tenacibaculum salmonis (sal.monis. L. gen. n. salmonis, of salmon, since it was isolated from Atlantic salmon).

Cells are Gram-stain-negative, rod-shaped and exhibit gliding motility. Degenerative spherical cells become abundant after 8days of culturing. Two novel species of the genus Novosphingobium (family Erythrobacteraceae, order Sphingomonadales, class Alphaproteobacteria, phylum Pseudomonadota, kingdom Pseudomonadati [1]) were described in the International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology in 2023, both using the same species epithet, Novosphingobium mangrovi. Hu et al. [2] published their description on 28 April 2023 for strain B2637T (=KCTC 72969T=MCCC 1K04460T; 16S rRNA gene: GenBank ON077585; genome assembly: GenBank GCA_022818885), while Huang et al. [3] published their description on 19 May 2023 for strain HK4-1T (=JCM 35764T=MCCC 1K08252T; 16S rRNA gene: GenBank OP458508; genome assembly: GenBank GCA_025153475). Although both strains were isolated from mangrove sediments, their pairwise 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity (97.5%), average nucleotide identity (84.7%) and digital DNADNA hybridization (21%; Formula 2) values were all below the recommended species delineation thresholds of 98.65%, 95% and 70% [4], respectively. Coupled with their clear separation on a core-genome phylogenomic tree (Fig. 1), these results collectively support their classification as two distinct species.

On the basis of the earlier valid publication, Novosphingobium mangrovi Hu et al. 2023 has priority over Novosphingobium mangrovi Huang et al. 2023. As per Rule 51b (5) of the International Code of Nomenclature of Prokaryotes [5], Novosphingobium mangrovi Huang et al. 2023 is, therefore, illegitimate, as the species epithet is a later homonym of Novosphingobium mangrovi Hu et al. 2023.
